newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudan's Mahdi warns investors against Khartoum.
newsitem.headline: Sudan's Mahdi warns investors against Khartoum.

text.p: Ousted Sudanese prime minister Sadeq al-Mahdi warned foreigners on Wednesday against investing in Sudan and said war will only increase until its Islamist government falls.

Mahdi told a news conference in Nairobi after talks with Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi and Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni that he was touring Africa to try to drum up support for international pressure to force Khartoum to negotiate.
Asked about rebels last week declaring foreign oil companies in Sudan as legitimate targets, he stopped short of directly endorsing attacks but said such a stand was understandable.

"This is the economic aspect of the conflict. I think it is very ill-advised for any company to do business with the current regime in Khartoum," said Mahdi, who fled to Eritrea from Khartoum in December after years of being under surveillance.
Sudanese President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir on Monday opened an oilfield in Upper Mile state in southern Sudan developed with the help of a Qatari partnership.
The Sudan Alliance Forces, a small rebel group in an Eritrea -based alliance of opposition movements, said last week it considered all foreign companies operation in Sudan as military targets.
The Sudan People's Liberation Army, the largest rebel group in the opposition alliance, has also said oil fields developed by a Canadian company were military targets for the rebels.
"It is only natural there is this tendency to expect all investors to withhold any kind of activity in Sudan until there is a basis for stability and peace," said Mahdi, leader of the Umma party.
He accused Khartoum of squandering Sudan's resources by devoting them to supporting the military and said foreign investors were opportunists who only aided the regime.
"The problem is one where violence, confrontation and regional and international involvment is going to increase...as long as this regime is in power," said the opposition leader.
"The war has spread and is going to spread more and more."
Mahdi said he believed a popular uprising would destroy the regime in Khartoum but he was visiting African states to explain how they could become involved in resolving the Sudan problem.
Bashir overthrew Mahdi's democratically elected government in a bloodless coup in 1989.
Mahdi denied accusations by Khartoum's Islamist government that Eritrean and Ethiopian troops fought alongside rebels in an offensive in eastern Sudan in January by the National Democratic Alliance.
He said he was pushing for a greater international role in the search for peace in Sudan by a committee chaired by Moi of the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development regional group.
He said he hoped peace efforts would have a greater international profile so that Khartoum would either have to bow finally to international pressure or isolate itself totally.
Mahdi said he had written to South African President Nelson Mandela and hoped to meet him because he wanted him to become involved in efforts to end the Sudan conflict.
Sudan has relations ranging from bad to bellicose with Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda. Western diplomats strongly doubt Bashir will be toppled by a popular uprising in Khartoum.
